To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pp60v-src and protein tyrosine kinases inhibit GABAA receptors, presumably by phosphorylation of the receptors.
pp60v-src is capable of phosphorylating GABAA receptors, and that the phosphorylation occurs in the large cytoplasmically located domains of the beta and gamma subunits.
the GABAA receptor is a substrate for tyrosine kinase and that tyrosine kinase activity is required for the GABA response of the receptor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of protein tyrosine kinases in the regulation of GABAA receptor function.
the role of phosphorylation in regulating GABAA receptor function.
the molecular basis of GABAA receptor function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tyrosine phosphorylation of the beta 2 subunit of the GABAA receptor may be involved in the regulation of receptor function.
tyrosine phosphorylation of the GABAA receptor by a tyrosine kinase is a mechanism that regulates the function of the receptor.

the phosphorylation of the GABAA receptor by tyrosine kinase is a mechanism of regulating GABA-gated chloride currents in a manner that is distinct from that of the phosphorylation of GABA-gated channels by protein kinase C.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
tyrosine kinase activity regulates GABA receptor function by phosphorylating the beta 2 subunit and the large loop of the gamma 2 subunit.
tyrosine phosphorylation is an additional mechanism for regulating GABAA receptor function.
GABAA receptors are tyrosine phosphorylated in vivo by pp60v-scr and that this phosphorylation modulates the GABA-elicited currents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tyrosine kinase phosphorylates GABA A receptors and this can affect their function.
protein tyrosine kinases can phosphorylate GABAA receptors and that this phosphorylation is important for the regulation of GABAA receptor function.
the phosphorylation of tyrosine residues of the GABAA receptor by tyrosine kinases can modulate GABAA receptor function.
